tldr: By combining GPU-native B-spline trajectory optimization with a path-retiming algorithm called TimeOpt, this framework plans executable motions in an astonishing 4.4 ms while satisfying torque limits and adapting to changing payloads.
hero_caption: Overview of the real-world manipulation pipeline running on a single RTX 6000 Ada GPU. Taking a distance field from the perception module (SceneFields) and candidates from grasp generation (GraspGenX), cuRoboV2-Fast plans grasp approach and lift motions in just 23 ms to drive the robot (YAM) at high speed.
overview:
Moving a robot arm quickly and safely requires balancing two goals: finding collision-free paths quickly (reducing planning latency) and driving the arm as fast as possible near its limits while respecting actuator torque and velocity constraints (reducing execution time). Grasping heavy objects drastically alters the system dynamics, meaning the geometrically shortest path is not necessarily the fastest traversal path. Considering payload-dependent torque limits is therefore essential. However, traditional trajectory planning that repeatedly runs inverse dynamics and collision checking within optimization loops takes too long, making real-time deployment difficult.

To tackle this, the authors developed cuRoboV2-Fast, a GPU-accelerated motion planner engineered to aggressively eliminate both planning latency and execution time. By adopting B-splines with local support for geometric trajectory representation, they drastically reduced optimization iterations. Alongside this, they introduced TimeOpt, which optimizes traversal speed while keeping the geometric path fixed. TimeOpt exploits spline local support to formulate banded linear systems, solving them with massive parallelism on the GPU to compute near-limit speed profiles in sub-milliseconds. Furthermore, it incorporates GPU hardware-tailored accelerations, including differentiable inverse dynamics that update payload inertial parameters without recompilation and axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) collision pruning.

In evaluation benchmarks with a Franka arm carrying a 3 kg payload, cuRoboV2-Fast achieved a mean planning time of 4.4 ms on an RTX 5090—$14.7\times$ faster than cuRoboV2. Even on an edge-oriented Jetson AGX Orin, it planned faster than previous desktop GPU configurations. In real-robot pick-and-drop tasks on YAM, motion planning accounted for only 1.0% of the total cycle time, demonstrating that planning computation is no longer the bottleneck.
contributions: Reduced the required initial iterations from 125 to 25 (a $5\times$ reduction) to reach the same success rate as cuRoboV1 by adopting B-spline trajectory optimization.
Developed TimeOpt, a GPU method that optimizes speed profiles up to velocity, acceleration, jerk, and torque limits along fixed paths using banded Newton systems.
Built fast differentiable inverse dynamics and kinematics routines that update payload inertial parameters instantly without kernel recompilation.
Implemented a GPU-parallel RRT that finds coarse collision-free initial paths in sub-milliseconds (0.305 ms on average) via synchronous rounds and CUDA graphs.
Integrated perception, grasp generation, and motion planning on a single GPU on the real robot YAM, reducing cycle time by 34.6% with planning taking only 1.0% of the cycle.

sections.heading: Why must we accelerate both planning and execution time?
sections.summary: Achieving fast manipulation requires not only slashing planning latency, but also generating trajectories that let the real hardware move near actuator constraint limits in the shortest possible time. This chapter introduces the impact of payload variations on robot dynamics, along with the core concepts and six main contributions of cuRoboV2-Fast.
sections.details:
When aiming for fast robotic manipulation, we run into two bottlenecks: slow trajectory planning computations and long trajectory execution times on physical hardware. Pushing an arm to move near its limits quickly runs into joint velocity, acceleration, and jerk boundaries, as well as the maximum torque limits of the actuators. Grasping a heavy payload drastically increases the moment of inertia. Running the same trajectory with a payload can cause torque overruns, resulting in desynchronization or emergency stops.

Moreover, the geometrically shortest path in Cartesian space is not necessarily the fastest path for the robot to traverse. Trajectories that pass through configurations where actuators have poor mechanical leverage must be slowed down significantly to stay within torque limits. Furthermore, uniform timestep scaling across the entire trajectory has a fundamental drawback: if a torque limit is reached at a single configuration, it unnecessarily slows down other sections of the trajectory that still have ample headroom.

cuRoboV2-Fast overcomes these challenges simultaneously using massive GPU parallelism. The paper highlights the following key contributions:
- Reduced optimization iterations via B-spline trajectory representations (dropping from 125 to 25 iterations compared to cuRoboV1).
- Introduction of TimeOpt, a GPU-parallel optimizer that pushes speed along a fixed path to its physical limits (further reducing execution time by 15.7% in 0.28 ms on average).
- Differentiable inverse dynamics modules that adapt instantly to changing payloads without kernel recompilation.
- A GPU-parallel RRT that discovers collision-free initial paths in a rapid 0.305 ms.
- Demonstrated overall planning times of 4.4 ms on an RTX 5090 and 26 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin.
- A 34.6% reduction in cycle time during a single-GPU deployment combining perception, grasping, and planning on the physical YAM robot.

sections.heading: The evolution of parallel planners and trajectory retiming
sections.summary: Recent advances in motion planning combine accelerated search using CPU SIMD or GPU parallelism with trajectory optimization and retiming techniques. This chapter reviews parallel RRT methods, B-spline smoothing, fixed-path dynamic scaling like TOPPRA, and differences in GPU dynamics implementations.
sections.details:
The history of fast motion planning is a continuous effort to adapt algorithms to parallel processor architectures. For initial path search, approaches like CPU SIMD-accelerated VAMP and GPU thread-distributed tree expansion in pRRTC have drastically shortened search times. The RRT in this paper also pursues GPU parallelism, but cleanly decouples tree expansion from constraint validation to easily accommodate additional constraint checks.

In post-search trajectory optimization (such as CHOMP and TrajOpt), B-spline representations have long been used for their smoothness and ease of local deformation. This work links the local support property of B-splines—where a given control point only influences a narrow segment—directly to GPU warp-level parallel reductions, maximizing gradient accumulation efficiency.

In the realm of path retiming to minimize traversal time along a fixed path, methods like TOPPRA and TOPP3 are well known. They leverage the property that path torque is affine in path acceleration and squared path velocity to solve sequences of small linear programs (LPs). TimeOpt in cuRoboV2-Fast also uses this dynamics reduction, but parameterizes squared velocity directly with a cubic B-spline and solves the resulting banded Newton system on the GPU using a primal-dual predictor-corrector method. By avoiding sequential processing like in TOPPRA, it achieves parallel execution in just 0.28 ms.

Compared to robot computation libraries like Pinocchio or GRiD, this system avoids relying entirely on source code generation. Instead, it passes link traversal schedules and inertial parameters as runtime data. As a result, changing payloads does not require recompiling GPU kernels, enabling immediate optimization under updated torque limits.

sections.heading: Under the hood: the high-speed architecture of cuRoboV2-Fast
sections.summary: The system rests on five pillars: parallel initial path search, B-spline trajectory optimization, fixed-path time optimization (TimeOpt), recompilation-free differentiable dynamics, and geometric pruning. Every step, from geometry generation to boundary-pushing time compression, is optimized for GPU memory hierarchies and thread structures.
sections.details:
The pipeline starts with a linear interpolation seed, runs RRT to find an initial path if obstacles are present, refines it into a smooth shape via B-spline optimization, and finally compresses traversal time to the physical limits using TimeOpt.

### III-A Collision-Free Initialization with RRT
When a linear seed cannot avoid collisions, a bidirectional RRT runs on the GPU in synchronous rounds. The proposed Nearest-Node kernel tiles both tree nodes and joint coordinates to find the nearest node via parallel reduction. Collision checking along all proposed edges is evaluated in batches, and valid prefixes (segments up to the first collision) are written to free slots via parallel scans. CUDA graphs and pre-allocated buffer reuse keep kernel dispatch overhead near zero.

### III-B B-Spline Trajectory Optimization
Trajectories are parameterized as uniform cubic B-splines. Under this formulation, the position, velocity, acceleration, and jerk of any sample point depend on only four adjacent control points. In the forward pass, sample-joint pairs are mapped to GPU threads and evaluated independently. In the backward pass, gradients are gathered only from the samples that each control point influences. Warp-level reductions sum control point gradients directly, avoiding heavy atomic additions and massive intermediate tensors.

### III-C TimeOpt: Fixed-Path Time Optimization
Once the geometric path $q(s)$ ($s \in [0, 1]$ being the path parameter) is determined, TimeOpt optimizes traversal speed without altering the path geometry. The squared path velocity $\dot{s}^2$ at parameter $s$ is parameterized by a clamped cubic B-spline $x_r(s)$. The objective function approximates traversal time via an integral of the inverse traversal speed (averaged over samples), constrained by upper and lower bounds on joint velocity, acceleration, jerk, and torque. Because the path is fixed, torque follows an exact affine relationship: $\tau(s) = A(s)\ddot{s} + D(s)\dot{s}^2 + g(s)$. Inverse dynamics only need to be evaluated three times per sample, requiring no recalculation during subsequent iterations. The Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions yield a block-banded Newton system, which converges to a local optimum in under 0.3 ms using a primal-dual predictor-corrector solver with direct Cholesky factorization on the GPU.

### III-D Accelerating Robot Computations and Geometric Pruning
Forward kinematics (FK) traverses link hierarchies in shared memory in tree order. In inverse kinematics (IK) gradient computation, wrenches (forces and torques) on each link are gathered in a single pass and projected simultaneously to each actuator, eliminating redundant ancestor traversals. For self-collision checks, axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABBs) are built on the fly around link collision spheres; if two AABBs do not overlap, all sphere-sphere checks between them are skipped. In swept collision checking against the environment, bounding boxes around the swept spheres prune unnecessary distance queries.

### III-E Differentiable Inverse Dynamics with Instant Payload Updates
Rather than relying on automated code generation, link execution schedules and inertial parameters are stored as runtime data. Independent unbranched chains are traversed locally by GPU workers and synchronized only across chain dependencies. Using the Recursive Newton-Euler Algorithm (RNEA) to compute torques, backward loss gradients are propagated directly to joint coordinates and spline control points without forming dense Jacobian matrices. When grasped objects change, updating mass, center of mass, and inertia tensor values immediately reflects into torque optimization without recompilation.

### III-F Integrated Grasp Planning
For candidate grasp poses, collision-aware IK is solved in batch to rank candidates by pose error and joint displacement. Rather than running multiple full trajectory optimizations, a single grasp pose is selected via fast IK, after which three consecutive trajectories are planned: reaching pre-grasp, linear approach along the grasp axis, and lifting.

sections.heading: Benchmark results: $14.7\times$ speedup and drastically reduced real-robot cycle times
sections.summary: Path search, optimization convergence, dynamics calculations, and physical manipulation were evaluated across a Franka arm, a Unitree G1 humanoid, and the custom YAM arm. The planner achieved a 4.4 ms mean planning time on an RTX 5090, outpaced desktop baselines even on a Jetson AGX Orin, and significantly reduced execution and cycle times on real hardware.
sections.details:
Experiments evaluated the 7-DOF Franka Panda, the 29-DOF Unitree G1, and the YAM robot.

### IV-A Path Initialization Performance
Across 2,575 queries in MotionBenchMaker and MPINets, the proposed RRT achieved a 98.68% initialization success rate. Mean computation time was just 0.305 ms, which is $43.0\times$ faster than cuRoboV1 PRM (13.09 ms) and $1.48\times$ faster than pRRTC (0.450 ms).

### IV-B Trajectory Optimization Convergence and TimeOpt Impact
In a 100-problem caged obstacle benchmark, cuRoboV1 required 125 initial L-BFGS iterations to reach a 93% success rate, whereas cuRoboV2-Fast reached 93% in only 25 iterations ($5\times$ iteration efficiency). Furthermore, applying TimeOpt to trajectories with uniform timestep reduction shortened mean execution time by an additional 15.7% (20.3% shorter compared to the unoptimized initial trajectory), demonstrating the importance of path retiming.

### IV-C Payload-Aware Motion Planning
When planning with a 3 kg payload, cuRoboV2-Fast averaged 4.43 ms on an RTX 5090—$14.7\times$ faster than cuRoboV2 (65.3 ms) and $10.0\times$ faster than cuRoboV1+TOPPRA. On the embedded Jetson AGX Orin, it finished in 25.99 ms, which is faster than cuRoboV1+TOPPRA running on an RTX 5090 (44.3 ms). Although geometric joint travel was slightly longer than cuRoboV1 (0.8% to 4.2% longer), accounting for torque constraints resulted in a 6.8% shorter physical execution time on average.

### IV-D Microbenchmarks for Robot Computations
At batch sizes of 1 and 1,024, forward and inverse kinematics were $1.1\times$ to $1.3\times$ faster than cuRoboV2, while Jacobian calculations on the G1 were approximately $38\times$ faster than cuRoboV1. Differentiable inverse dynamics was $6.4\times$ faster on G1 than code-generated GRiD, and $1.5\times$ faster than single-batch CPU Pinocchio. AABB pruning accelerated self-collision checking on G1 by roughly $52\times$ compared to cuRoboV1.

### IV-E & F Simulation Experiments and Payload Adaptation
In a 5-cube clearing simulation with YAM, the mean planning time per cube was 26.05 ms ($11.2\times$ faster than cuRoboV2), reducing execution time by 46.6%. Comparing 100 g and 800 g payloads showed that with the heavier load, the planner naturally shifted motion toward joint 5 to avoid torque violations at joint 2.

### IV-G Real-Robot Deployment
Deploying on the YAM robot alongside stereo perception (SceneFields) and grasp generation (GraspGenX) on a single RTX 6000 Ada, the proportion of time operating at 90–100% of maximum velocity nearly doubled compared to cuRoboV2. Arm execution time decreased by 44.8%, reducing total cycle time to 5.93 s (a 34.6% reduction). Motion planning took only 0.06 s, representing just 1.0% of the cycle, proving that planning is no longer the bottleneck.

sections.heading: Beyond planning latency: shifting focus to manipulation's next bottlenecks
sections.summary: Accelerating planning algorithms has compressed motion planning latency to just 1% of total cycle time. This shift demonstrates that the real key to shortening cycle times lies in generating trajectories that fully exploit actuator limits, shifting future research toward robust contact and grasping.
sections.details:
The primary impact of cuRoboV2-Fast is turning torque-limited, collision-free trajectory optimization—long considered one of the heaviest computation blocks in robotics—into a routine tool that completes in a few milliseconds, far faster than typical perception update cycles.

Now that planning accounts for only 1% of the total cycle (around 60 ms), squeezing a few extra milliseconds out of planning algorithms will have negligible impact on real-world operational speed. Instead, the focus shifts to generating trajectories that extract 100% of the physical hardware's capability. As demonstrated in this study, maximizing sustained high-speed motion by combining dynamics with TimeOpt rather than pursuing geometrically shortest paths directly translates to shorter execution times.

Furthermore, achieving 26 ms planning times on edge processors like the Jetson AGX Orin represents a major milestone for onboard control in autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) and humanoids. The authors conclude that rather than planning latency, contact-rich interaction and robust grasp pose selection to prevent grasp failures will be the main battleground for improving manipulation cycle times.

takeaways: The geometrically shortest path is not always the fastest. When actuator torque limits are tight, taking a slightly longer route that accounts for dynamics gets the robot to its goal sooner.
Aligning B-spline local support with GPU warp structures and shared memory eliminates large intermediate gradient tensors and atomic adds, dramatically boosting optimization efficiency.
Fixed-path time optimization (TimeOpt) combines affine dynamics reduction with banded Newton solvers to cut execution times by over 15% with sub-0.3 ms latency.
Because planning now takes only 1% of the cycle, the primary focus for overall system speedup has shifted from planning latency to trajectory quality near motor limits and reliable grasp contact.
limitations: TimeOpt and trajectory optimization rely on local gradient-based optimization, offering no theoretical guarantee of global optimality.

Grasp planning uses fast IK checks to pick a single representative pose instead of optimizing trajectories across all candidates, which may miss feasible approach trajectories in tight, cluttered spaces.
As cycle times shrink on physical hardware, contact-rich interactions—such as physical gripper actuation delays and slippage during contact—have emerged as the dominant system bottlenecks.
